levels.title: Rome in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the three big eras of Roman history and roughly when each began and ended.

levels.title: Romulus and Remus
levels.objective: After this level you can retell Rome's founding legend and explain why Romans valued it.

levels.title: What the Ground Remembers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what archaeology shows about Rome's earliest villages.

levels.title: Seven Hills and a River
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Tiber and the seven hills shaped where and why Rome grew.

levels.title: The Etruscans Next Door
levels.objective: After this level you can describe who the Etruscans were and what Rome borrowed from them.

levels.title: The Seven Kings
levels.objective: After this level you can outline Rome's age of kings and how kingship worked there.

levels.title: Gods of the Household and the State
levels.objective: After this level you can describe early Roman religion, from household spirits to state priests and omens.

levels.title: The Roman Family
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the power of the paterfamilias and how Roman families were organized.

levels.title: The Last King
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome overthrew Tarquin the Proud and why it rejected kings.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Rome Began
levels.objective: After this level you can connect Rome's geography, neighbors, legends and kings into one founding story.

levels.title: A Republic Is Born
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a republic is and what SPQR stood for.

levels.title: Two Consuls, One Year
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how consuls shared power and why their terms were short.

levels.title: The Senate
levels.objective: After this level you can describe who sat in the Senate and how it steered the Republic.

levels.title: Patricians and Plebeians
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Conflict of the Orders between Rome's old families and ordinary citizens.

levels.title: The Twelve Tables
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Rome wrote down its laws and what that changed.

levels.title: Tribunes of the Plebs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the tribunes' power to protect plebeians, including the veto.

levels.title: Cincinnatus and the Citizen Ideal
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the story of Cincinnatus and explain the Roman idea of civic duty.

levels.title: The Gauls Sack Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Gallic sack of Rome and how it changed Roman defense.

levels.title: Conquering Italy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome came to control the Italian peninsula, and the role of roads and alliances.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How the Republic Worked
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how consuls, Senate, assemblies and tribunes balanced one another.

levels.title: Carthage, Queen of the Sea
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Carthage and why it clashed with Rome.

levels.title: The First Punic War
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome built a navy and won the First Punic War.

levels.title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
levels.objective: After this level you can retell Hannibal's march over the Alps with his army and elephants.

levels.title: Disaster at Cannae
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened at Cannae and why it is still studied.

levels.title: Fabius the Delayer
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Fabius Maximus's strategy of avoiding battle and why it worked.

levels.title: Scipio and Zama
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal at Zama.

levels.title: Rome Turns East
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Rome came to dominate Greece and the Hellenistic kingdoms.

levels.title: Carthage Must Be Destroyed
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how and why Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE.

levels.title: The Legion
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how a Roman legion was organized, equipped and trained.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Master of the Mediterranean
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Punic Wars turned Rome into a Mediterranean power.

levels.title: The Gracchi Brothers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the land reforms of the Gracchi and why they ended in violence.

levels.title: Marius Remakes the Army
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Marius's reforms tied soldiers to their generals.

levels.title: Sulla Marches on Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Sulla's march on Rome broke a taboo.

levels.title: Spartacus
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the slave revolt led by Spartacus and how it ended.

levels.title: Pompey the Great
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Pompey's rise and his conquests in the East.

levels.title: Cicero Against Catiline
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Catiline conspiracy and Cicero's role as consul.

levels.title: The First Triumvirate
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the informal alliance of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus.

levels.title: Caesar in Gaul
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Caesar's conquest of Gaul and why it made him so powerful.

levels.title: Crossing the Rubicon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why crossing the Rubicon meant civil war.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Ides of March
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Caesar's dictatorship, his assassination, and why the Republic still did not survive.

levels.title: Octavian, Caesar's Heir
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Caesar's young heir built power after the assassination.

levels.title: Antony and Cleopatra
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the alliance of Mark Antony and Cleopatra and why it alarmed Rome.

levels.title: Actium
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Battle of Actium and its consequences.

levels.title: Augustus, First Emperor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Augustus ruled as emperor while claiming to restore the Republic.

levels.title: The Pax Romana
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Pax Romana and what peace made possible.

levels.title: A City of Marble
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Augustus rebuilt Rome and why buildings mattered politically.

levels.title: Virgil and the Aeneid
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the Aeneid is and why Augustus's Rome valued it.

levels.title: Months Named for Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Julian calendar and how July and August got their names.

levels.title: Teutoburg Forest
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the disaster in the Teutoburg Forest and how it fixed the Rhine frontier.

levels.title: Milestone: From Republic to Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Rome's path from republic to empire and explain what changed and what stayed.

levels.title: Tiberius
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the reign of Tiberius and the problem of succession.

levels.title: Caligula
levels.objective: After this level you can separate what is known about Caligula from later rumor.

levels.title: Claudius Conquers Britain
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Claudius's reign and the invasion of Britain.

levels.title: Nero and the Great Fire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Great Fire of Rome and Nero's reputation.

levels.title: The Year of the Four Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened in 69 CE and what it revealed about imperial power.

levels.title: The Flavians and the Colosseum
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Flavian dynasty and the building of the Colosseum.

levels.title: Pompeii and Vesuvius
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the eruption of Vesuvius and why Pompeii is so valuable to historians.

levels.title: Trajan's Empire at Its Largest
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Trajan's conquests and the empire at its greatest extent.

levels.title: Hadrian and His Wall
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Hadrian consolidated the frontiers and built his wall.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Five Good Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the era of the Five Good Emperors, ending with Marcus Aurelius.

levels.title: A Day in the City
levels.objective: After this level you can describe daily life in the city of Rome, from apartment blocks to the forum.

levels.title: Slavery in Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how slavery shaped Roman society and what freed slaves could become.

levels.title: Bread and Circuses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the grain dole and public games and why rulers provided them.

levels.title: Gladiators
levels.objective: After this level you can separate the reality of gladiator fights from popular myth.

levels.title: Chariot Racing
levels.objective: After this level you can describe chariot racing, the Circus Maximus and the racing factions.

levels.title: The Baths
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Roman baths were like and why they mattered socially.

levels.title: What Romans Ate
levels.objective: After this level you can describe what rich and poor Romans ate, including garum.

levels.title: Latin, the Language That Lived On
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Latin spread and became the Romance languages.

levels.title: Roman Women
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the rights and roles of Roman women, and their limits.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Everyday Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can connect housing, work, food, entertainment and religion into a picture of daily life.

levels.title: All Roads Lead to Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Roman roads were built and why they mattered.

levels.title: Aqueducts
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how aqueducts carried water to Roman cities using gravity.

levels.title: Roman Concrete
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what made Roman concrete so durable.

levels.title: The Pantheon
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Pantheon and its record-breaking dome.

levels.title: Running the Provinces
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how governors, taxes and local elites ran the provinces.

levels.title: Becoming Roman
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Roman citizenship and how it spread to all free people in 212.

levels.title: Roman Law
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the key ideas of Roman law and how they reached modern legal systems.

levels.title: Money and Trade
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Roman coins, trade routes and the economy of the Mediterranean.

levels.title: Life on the Frontier
levels.objective: After this level you can describe forts, soldiers and communities on the Roman frontier.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Rome Held an Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how roads, law, citizenship, the army and trade held the empire together.

levels.title: The Crisis of the Third Century
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the chaos of the third century, when emperors rose and fell rapidly.

levels.title: Diocletian Divides the Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Diocletian's reforms and the Tetrarchy.

levels.title: The First Christians
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Christianity began and spread through the Roman world.

levels.title: Persecution
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why and when Christians were persecuted by the Roman state.

levels.title: Constantine
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Constantine's rise and his support for Christianity.

levels.title: Constantinople
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Constantine founded a new capital on the Bosporus.

levels.title: Julian the Apostate
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Julian's attempt to restore the old religion.

levels.title: A Christian Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity became the empire's official religion under Theodosius.

levels.title: Disaster at Adrianople
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Gothic victory at Adrianople and why it mattered.

levels.title: Checkpoint: A Changed Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the empire of 395 differed from the empire of Augustus.

levels.title: The Sack of Rome, 410
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Alaric's sack of Rome and its shock to the Roman world.

levels.title: Attila and the Huns
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Huns under Attila and their impact on the empire.

levels.title: 476: The Last Western Emperor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened in 476 and why historians debate its importance.

levels.title: Why Did Rome Fall?
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the main explanations for the fall of the Western Empire.

levels.title: The Empire That Didn't Fall
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Eastern Roman Empire lasted until 1453.

levels.title: Integration: Rome in Our Laws and Governments
levels.objective: After this level you can connect Roman institutions to modern republics and legal systems.

levels.title: Integration: Rome in Our Words, Calendars and Cities
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Rome's legacy in languages, calendars, architecture and city planning.

levels.title: Integration: How We Know About Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how historians use texts, inscriptions, coins and archaeology to study Rome.

levels.title: Integration: The Arc of Roman History
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the major turning points of Roman history into one story.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: Ancient Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Ancient Rome Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
